about.text: Milk in which the lactose has been split into glucose and galactose by the enzyme lactase, or largely removed by membranes, so that people who cannot digest lactose can drink it. It tastes sweeter than ordinary milk.

sources.text: The first paragraph of its article, shortened.
The photograph, its author and its licence, from its page.

facts.v: Lactose-free means under 0.1 g lactose per 100 g

A little yeast lactase is injected through a sterile 0.22 µm filter into the sterile, packed UHT milk; hydrolysis is complete after 7–10 days at room temperature. Yeast lactase does not survive 135 °C, so it cannot go in before UHT unless it is dosed again afterwards

Valio filters the milk, takes the lactose out, puts proteins, minerals and fat back and hydrolyses the rest; Wikipedia says ultrafiltration, Valio's wiki entry says chromatographic separation (conflict, unresolved)
Hydrolysis makes the milk taste sweeter (lactose is far less sweet than glucose and galactose); a patent says consumers notice it at about 80 % hydrolysis
Added before pasteurising or UHT; the milk is held at the enzyme temperature until the lactose is gone, within the plant's 72 h holding limit (Cornell patent description)
